scope: Major figures of the Indian independence movement — seed batch (v1).

people.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
people.summary: Lawyer, activist, architect of mass non-violent resistance — the political method that made the freedom movement.

track.tooltip: Called to the bar at Inner Temple, 1891
track.summary: Three years in London. Vegetarian Society, theosophy, and a quiet shy man learning courtroom English.
track.note: Returns to India weeks later. Briefs are scarce; he sails for Durban in 1893 to argue a single case for Dada Abdulla & Co.

track.tooltip: Thrown off the train at Pietermaritzburg, 1893
track.summary: First-class ticket holder ejected for being non-white. The night Gandhi later cited as the moment he committed to political action.
track.note: Twenty-one years in South Africa follow. The satyagraha method is invented in those years, before any of it reaches India.

track.tooltip: Returns to India, lands at Apollo Bunder, 1915
track.summary: Forty-five years old. Gokhale tells him to spend the first year travelling India in third-class trains and saying nothing.
track.note: He more or less obeys. The political year begins in 1917 at Champaran.

track.summary: Bihar's indigo planters had locked tenants into ruinous contracts for a century. Gandhi's first Indian campaign broke them.
track.note: Arrested for refusing a magistrate's order to leave the district. The local court had to dismiss the case after thousands of peasants assembled. Provincial recognition of his method follows.

track.summary: An ashram on the banks of the Sabarmati outside Ahmedabad, run on satyagraha and self-spun cloth. The political base for the next 13 years.
track.note: He vows not to return until India is free. He never does — leaves on the Salt March in 1930 and the ashram is shut down by the Raj that year.

track.role: Architect of the campaign; surrendered his Kaiser-i-Hind medal and built the boycott machinery.
track.note: His first claim on the entire national movement. Most senior Congress leaders had wanted to wait for Dyer to be punished. Gandhi did not.

track.summary: Six-year sentence for sedition after Chauri Chaura. Released in 1924 for an appendicitis operation; spends the rest of the decade out of mass politics.
track.note: Trial speech at Ahmedabad: 'I am here to invite and submit cheerfully to the highest penalty.' Judge Broomfield called it the proudest day of his career.

track.role: Led the march from Sabarmati to Dandi at sixty-one — 78 satyagrahis, 24 days, 240 miles.
track.note: The deliberate slowness was the strategy. Twelve miles a day to maximise press coverage and recruit walkers from villages along the route. Photographed daily for the world's papers.

track.summary: Ended his fast-unto-death against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Negotiated with Ambedkar through Yerwada's prison bars.
track.note: A reserved-seat compromise rather than separate electorates. Ambedkar always treated it as a settlement under duress; Gandhi treated it as a moral correction.

track.summary: Moves from Sabarmati to a tiny village near Wardha. Deliberately central, deliberately remote. Stays nearly a decade.
track.note: Run more austerely than Sabarmati. Visiting senior Congress leaders had to fetch their own water and clean their own latrines.

track.role: 'Do or die' at Gowalia Tank Maidan; arrested before dawn the next morning along with the entire Congress leadership.
track.note: Spends the rest of the war at the Aga Khan Palace, Pune. Kasturba dies there in 1944, four months before his release.

track.summary: Walked barefoot through villages where the previous month's communal killings had emptied the houses. He was 77.
track.note: Forty-seven villages on foot in four months. While the Congress in Delhi negotiated partition, he was trying to remind Bengal what it had been before October.

track.summary: Shot at point-blank range during the evening prayer meeting. He was on a fast for communal harmony at the time of his death.
track.note: Three bullets from a Beretta. Nehru on All India Radio: 'The light has gone out of our lives.' India observed 13 days of mourning. Five months later, the Republic was a year and a half away.

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.summary: Congress president, prime minister, principal architect of the Indian republic and its first seventeen years.

track.summary: Sent to England at fifteen. Two years at Harrow, three at Trinity Cambridge, two at the Inner Temple.
track.note: He read science at Trinity. The political education was incidental — Sinn Féin pamphlets, Fabian lectures, the Russian revolution of 1905 read in the Cambridge papers.

track.tooltip: First meets Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress, 1916
track.summary: Twenty-six and looking for a politics. Gandhi was already forty-six and three years into Champaran preparation.
track.note: Underwhelmed initially. Three years later at Champaran the method made sense. By 1921 he was running Non-Cooperation in the United Provinces.

track.role: Provincial leader for the United Provinces; first imprisonment Lucknow Jail 1921.
track.note: Shed the Theosophical-Society polish; came out of jail a recognisable Congress nationalist.

track.summary: First sustained contact with the international anti-colonial Left. Returns convinced India's freedom is part of a wider settlement.
track.note: Meets Sun Yat-sen's widow, Albert Einstein's correspondence, and the African delegations. The internationalism shaped his later non-aligned line as prime minister.

track.role: Congress president, the youngest in its history. Unfurled the tricolour at midnight on 31 December.
track.note: His father Motilal handed him the chair. Seen at the time as nepotism; in retrospect it was the moment Congress committed to Purna Swaraj rather than dominion status.

track.role: Arrested at the start of the campaign; spent two of the next four years in Naini Jail.
track.note: Did not march himself. The pattern of long imprisonments was set: nine years in jail, total, before independence.

track.tooltip: The Discovery of India written at Ahmednagar Fort, 1942–46
track.summary: Three years in a princely-state fort with twelve other Congressmen. The book that defined the post-independence vision was written there in pencil.
track.note: Published 1946. The middle chapters — on syncretism, on what India had been before colonial rule — became the secular republic's founding myth.

track.role: Delivered 'Tryst with Destiny' to the Constituent Assembly hours before midnight on 14 August.
track.note: The speech does not mention partition. Mountbatten was sworn in as Governor-General the next morning; Nehru as the first Prime Minister.

track.summary: Died in office, prime minister for nearly seventeen continuous years. The country had not known another.
track.note: The building became the Nehru Memorial Museum in 1966 and remained that for fifty-seven years. Renamed Prime Ministers' Museum in 2023.

people.name: Bhagat Singh
people.summary: Revolutionary, theorist, and martyr at twenty-three. Argued Marxism in jail and went to the gallows reading Lenin.

track.tooltip: National College, Lahore — left Congress for revolution, 1923
track.summary: Left Khalsa High School after his family's mortgage went to the British. National College was the polemical cousin of Lahore's Government College.
track.note: Read Bakunin, Trotsky, the Irish brigade. The college was a recruiting ground for the Hindustan Republican Association.

track.tooltip: HSRA founded at Firoz Shah Kotla, Delhi, 1928
track.summary: The Hindustan Republican Association becomes the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. The 'S' was Bhagat Singh's insertion.
track.note: First Indian revolutionary group to declare a socialist economic programme. The shift from anti-colonial nationalism to anti-capitalism made it dangerous to Congress as much as to the Raj.

track.summary: Killed assistant superintendent J.P. Saunders to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai. Their target had been the senior officer Scott; they shot the wrong man.
track.note: Posters appeared the next morning: 'Lala Lajpat Rai has been avenged.' The HSRA had carried out a political execution; the Raj read it as terrorism.

track.tooltip: Bombs the Central Legislative Assembly, Delhi, 8 April 1929
track.summary: Two non-lethal bombs into an empty corner of the chamber, plus leaflets, plus a deliberate refusal to escape. The trial was the point.
track.note: Inspired by Auguste Vaillant's bombing of the French Chamber. 'It takes a loud voice to make the deaf hear.' Arrested at the scene by choice.

track.summary: Demanded political-prisoner status — books, newspapers, decent food. Co-prisoner Jatin Das died on day 63.
track.note: The strike turned a terrorism trial into a national movement. Provincial assemblies adjourned. Congress paid for Das's funeral procession to Calcutta — half a million walked.

track.tooltip: Hanged at Lahore Central Jail, 23 March 1931
track.summary: Executed eleven hours ahead of schedule, an act the colonial state did not bother to explain. Bodies cremated secretly on the Sutlej.
track.note: Gandhi's silence on the executions during the Gandhi–Irwin negotiations cost him with the Punjab youth for a decade. Bhagat Singh's last book request: Lenin's State and Revolution.

people.name: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
people.summary: Jurist, economist, principal drafter of the Indian Constitution, and the most consequential anti-caste theorist of the twentieth century.

track.summary: First Mahar to matriculate from Elphinstone. Sat outside the classroom for fear his caste would defile its interior.
track.note: Sponsored by Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda. The Maharaja's scholarship took him to Columbia three years later.

track.summary: MA and PhD in economics under John Dewey. The lasting influence — democracy as a method of associated living, not a constitutional form.
track.note: The Columbia thesis became 'Castes in India' (1916), his first published anti-caste work. Dewey's influence is visible in every later constitutional speech.

track.summary: Doctorate in economics, called to the bar at Gray's Inn. The full apparatus a colonial subject could acquire.
track.note: Returned to India in 1917, ran out of scholarship money, taught at Sydenham College, returned to London in 1920 to finish. The compressed schedule produced a DSc, a barrister's qualification, and twenty pounds in pocket on arrival back.

track.summary: Led ten thousand Mahars to drink from the public tank at Mahad. The first organised Dalit assertion of access to a shared resource.
track.note: The tank's water was 'purified' by upper-caste rituals after the satyagraha. In December he returned and burnt the Manusmriti — the public renunciation of Hindu scriptural authority.

track.summary: Represented the Depressed Classes against Gandhi's Congress. Fought for separate electorates as constitutional protection.
track.note: The Communal Award of 1932 granted separate electorates. Gandhi began his fast-unto-death from Yerwada in protest. Ambedkar conceded under duress at the Poona Pact.

track.summary: Reserved seats inside a joint electorate, in exchange for ending Gandhi's fast. Ambedkar always read it as a settlement at gunpoint.
track.note: He wrote later: 'There was nothing noble in the fast. It was a foul and filthy act.' The reserved-seat compromise has shaped Indian electoral arithmetic ever since.

track.tooltip: Annihilation of Caste, drafted at Bombay, 1936
track.summary: An undelivered speech that became the canonical anti-caste text. The Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal cancelled the lecture rather than hear it.
track.note: Self-published when no Hindu reformist body would print it. Gandhi's response, and Ambedkar's reply to Gandhi, are appended in later editions.

track.role: Chair of the drafting committee of the Constitution; law minister in the first Cabinet.
track.note: Drafted in two years and eleven months. He called it 'a beautiful piece of paper' and said in 1953 he would be the first to burn it if it failed Dalits.

track.tooltip: Conversion to Buddhism, Diksha Bhoomi, 14 October 1956
track.summary: Took the refuges and the precepts at Nagpur with 380,000 Mahars. Twenty-two vows rejecting the Hindu pantheon.
track.note: He had announced the conversion intent in 1935 ('I was born a Hindu, but I shall not die a Hindu'). Took twenty-one years to find the form. He died fifty-three days later.

track.tooltip: Death at Alipur Road, New Delhi, 6 December 1956
track.summary: Died at home in his sleep, six weeks after the conversion at Nagpur. The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously the next year.
track.note: Cremation at Dadar Chowpatty, Bombay. Bharat Ratna conferred posthumously in 1990, thirty-four years late.

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.summary: Lawyer, Congress moderate, Muslim League president, and architect of partition. Founder and first Governor-General of Pakistan.

track.summary: Bar at sixteen, the youngest Indian called in his year. Watched Dadabhai Naoroji's election to the Commons.
track.note: Returned to Bombay 1896 to a slow practice. The legal style — meticulous, dispassionate, English-coded — became the lifelong manner.

track.summary: Calcutta session, the moderate wing under Naoroji. Speeches in flawless English on civil-service reform.
track.note: Naoroji's private secretary at the session. For the next fifteen years the most prominent Muslim figure in Congress, often called 'the ambassador of Hindu–Muslim unity'.

track.summary: Negotiated joint Congress–League demands for self-government. The high-water mark of his Hindu–Muslim coalition politics.
track.note: League accepted Congress's larger numbers; Congress accepted separate Muslim electorates. The bargain Gandhi's later mass politics rendered illegible to both sides.

track.summary: Walked out over Non-Cooperation. Booed off the stage when he addressed Gandhi as 'Mister' rather than 'Mahatma'.
track.note: He read mass agitation as ungovernable. 'Your way is the wrong way.' Two decades of constitutional politics follow before he reaches the Lahore Resolution.

track.summary: Practised at the Privy Council. Treated India as a closed file. Returned only when Liaquat Ali Khan persuaded him the League needed him.
track.note: He kept a Bombay flat for the eventual return. The years of distance gave him the political detachment to refuse Gandhi's later coalition offers.

track.summary: Demanded 'independent states' in the Muslim-majority regions. The constitutional position that became Pakistan.
track.note: The resolution did not name Pakistan; that came in journalism that month. The text spoke of 'states' (plural) in the east and west. The two-nation theory had its constitutional vehicle.

track.role: Issued the call. The League's response to the failed Cabinet Mission Plan.
track.note: He framed it as constitutional protest. The Calcutta provincial League read it as licence. The Great Calcutta Killings followed within hours of the date.

track.tooltip: Inaugural address to Pakistan Constituent Assembly, 11 August 1947
track.summary: 'You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques.' The secular speech the new state never made canonical.
track.note: The text was suppressed in Pakistani textbooks for decades. Reads in retrospect as an abandoned constitutional path — religion as private matter, citizenship as universal. He died thirteen months later.

track.tooltip: Death at the Governor-General's House, Karachi, 11 September 1948
track.summary: Tuberculosis the British knew about and Jinnah hid through the partition negotiations. Died thirteen months after Pakistan's founding.
track.note: Lord Wavell wrote in 1946 that he would have refused partition had he known how ill Jinnah was. The British did know. The political timing was made to fit a man too ill to manage delay.
